newsitem.title: USA: Billionaire puts Marlins baseball team up for sale.
newsitem.headline: Billionaire puts Marlins baseball team up for sale.

text.p: Billionaire Wayne Huizenga put the Florida Marlins up for sale Thursday, saying the economics of baseball made it nearly impossible for new Major League Baseball teams to make money.
Huizenga and his family have spent more than $200 million on the Marlins and see no likelihood of profits, the Florida businessman said at a news conference.
"My heart does not want me to sell, but my business sense says to sell," he said.

The Marlins are the second professional baseball team to be put up for sale this year. In January, Peter O'Malley, president and controlling owner of the Los Angeles Dodgers, said his family was putting the Dodgers up for sale.
O'Malley is believed to be close to a deal with Rupert Murdoch regarding the sale of the Dodgers.

Huizenga, a leading south Florida figure celebrated for his successes building trash hauler Waste Management Corp. and Blockbuster Video during its fast-growth years, also owns the Miami Dolphins football team, the Florida Panthers hockey team and the Pro Player stadium near Fort Lauderdale. He said he has no plans to sell those properties.

Launched with much fanfare five years ago amid hopes of catering to south Florida's large Hispanic population, the Marlins are Florida's only Major League team and will lose $30 million in 1997 despite a winning season so far, Huizenga said.
"The fact is that over the past years we have lost a lot of money," Huizenga said.

He said he had hired a law firm to solicit and evaluate bids for the Marlins but had made no contact with potential buyers. He declined to specify his asking price, but one published estimate valued the Marlins at $123 million.
"It's worth whatever anyone will pay for it," Huizenga said.

He said he would favour buyers who intended to keep the franchise in Florida but could not guarantee new owners would do so. Such a move would have to be approved by Major League Baseball's ruling board, he said.
The team is currently in second place in the National League East, behind the Atlanta Braves. The Marlins have won 45 games and lost 30 this season.

The Marlins have seen average attendance at home games in Pro Player Stadium, a venue designed for U.S. football, rise sharply to about 29,000. Many baseball fans say the Marlins need a stadium designed for baseball.

But after Huizenga hired top-performing and expensive players last winter, the Marlin's team payroll rose to $49.5 million a year. He said profits related to the Marlins at his stadium and a regional cable-television service he owns do little to offset the team's operating losses.
"This is not the fans' fault," Huizenga said. "When it comes to the Marlins, we have not been good businessmen."
Marlins President Don Smiley said the most likely buyers would be a large group of wealthy executives willing to tolerate sustained losses.
"The economics of baseball are underwater," Smiley told reporters. "The relationship between revenues and expenses ... there is no relationship."
Huizenga said other, successful baseball teams in Colorado and Ohio had much higher attendance at venues better suited for baseball, as well as lower costs.
Huizenga, also chairman of Republic Industries Inc., a services conglomerate, said he hoped to sell the team by the start of the 1998 baseball season next spring.
